paras: The hanging of Herb Crater was a nonfatal hanging in the autumn of 1880, reported from Wamega, Kansas, in which a group of masked men took Crater from jail at night and hung him from the joists of an opera house. Crater said the men wanted him to tell what he knew about horse thieving and let him live when he would not, and the only report of the episode is a short Wamega Tribune item reprinted in the Topeka Tribune.

On a Tuesday shortly before 6 November 1880, Walt Atkins entered Simpson's saloon, where Crater was playing billiards, and induced him to "try on a pair of iron bracelets." Crater was jailed, and the item said he was suspected of being a "spotter" for a gang of horse thieves.

According to Crater, a "mob of masked men" took him out of the jail that night and hung him from the joists of the opera house to make him tell what he knew about horse thieving. He said that he "wouldn't peach, or knew nothing to peach," and that the men then let him live. The Wamega Tribune noted that the jail had been broken open and that marks about Crater's head indicated "his story might be true."
Crater was then taken to Louisville "to await developments." The item names none of the masked men, and no report of arrests, an inquiry or later proceedings appears in the coverage.

The Topeka Tribune ran the item on 6 November 1880 in its "Kansas News" column, credited to the Wamega Tribune, among briefs on crops, county affairs, a saloon shooting and a jail break. It told the story in light slang, saying Crater was "jugged" and would not "peach," and treated his claim with guarded credence while offering no comment on the masked men. The item gives no race for Crater or his attackers and draws no connection between the hanging and race.
